newsitem.title: USA: California police baffled by smashing mystery.
newsitem.headline: California police baffled by smashing mystery.

text.p: It is a massive whodunnit that has had police baffled for a month: who is smashing the rear windows of hundreds of cars and trucks driving along Los Angeles freeways, and how are they doing it?
So far the mystery vandals have shattered the rear windows of 238 vehicles since Sept. 11. Police have not only failed to catch them, they are not even sure what weapon is being used.

Theories range from pellet guns to slingshots and even laser guns. Only one thing is certain -- the assailants are not armed with rifles or pistols, and so far, police say with a sigh of relief, no one has been killed or injured.

In an area where fatal drive-by freeway shootings were common a few years ago, authorities are alarmed at this new crime wave. Los Angeles City and County administrations have offered a reward of $35,000 for information leading to the arrests of suspects and local television station KCBS and its radio affiliate, KNX, have offered a $10,000 reward.
California Gov. Pete Wilson has vowed to prosecute the vandals "to the fullest extent of the law," including trying them for murder if anyone is killed in the incidents.

Ted Goldstein, spokesman for the city attorney's office, said a suspect tried for misdemeanor vandalism would face 12 months in prison on each count, but if a group is involved its members could be charged with felony conspiracy, which carries a minimum of three years in prison on each count.

"It's definitely a major problem out there," California Highway Patrol (CHP) spokesman Ed Ayabarreno said. "One of our main concerns is that a driver, being shocked by his rear window suddenly being shattered, might panic and swerve into another vehicle, causing a major accident."

The CHP, which patrols the state's freeways, has formed a special Vandalism Apprehension Force to hunt down the window smashers with beefed-up ground and air patrols and a hotline for motorists who have been attacked or have seen an attack.

But the CHP has been unable to stop the vandalism and has no clues as to who the vandals might be, Ayabarreno said. "So far we only have one piece of evidence and that's a marble found in the rear of one of the vehicles attacked. But we don't know for certain that was the projectile that did the damage," he said.

He said investigators were leaning toward the theory that the weapons being used in the attacks were pellet guns. "A pellet from a gun has enough velocity to shatter a tempered glass window, giving a spider's web effect, but not enough force to actually penetrate the glass, so it bounces off and that's probably why we haven't been able to recover them."
But he said slingshots and laser guns have not been ruled out.

Highway patrol officers questioned two men in the suburb of Inglewood on Monday night after a motorist saw them shining a laser light from their car. Officers determined that the laser, a "sighting" device, was not powerful enough to shatter a window, but it started investigators theorising that the vandals might use an industrial laser gun.

A 19-year-old woman arrested on a robbery warrant on Tuesday was being questioned in connection with the vandalism on Wednesday after the CHP received a tip that she may have had something to do with it, Ayabarreno said.

The attacks have occurred over a wide area of Los Angeles County, often at almost the same time but several miles (kilometres) apart, leading police to believe there are a number of copycat gangs committing them.
"We think that originally there was only one group of people involved, but once their actions started to receive publicity in the local media others started copying them," Ayabarreno said.
